papers.title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
papers.abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

papers.title: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
papers.abstract: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods. Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.

papers.title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
papers.abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

papers.title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (Padj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (Padj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (Padj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1. In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both PFDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (PFDR = 2.4 x 10-), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, Punadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

papers.title: CellVocal Attributes Transcriptional Dynamics to Spatial Signalling
papers.abstract: Understanding how local signalling shapes cell-state transitions requires linking spatial context to transcriptional dynamics. Here we present CellVocal, a framework that integrates spatial RNA velocity with cell-cell communication to decompose cell-state transitions into intrinsic and communication-associated components and further attribute their contributions to signalling modules and neighbouring sender cells. CellVocal recovered complex trajectories and communication perturbations in simulations and reconstructed coherent dynamics and spatially restricted ligand-receptor programmes across the mouse brain, gut and lung. Further analyses linked inferred NCAM1-NCAM1 signalling to lower cell-cycle-associated RNA velocity during embryonic neurogenesis. In melanoma, inferred local MIF-CD74+CD44 signalling corresponded to a predicted decline in the melanocytic programme. Analysis of acute liver failure identified hepatocyte-derived ANGPTL4-SDC1 signalling in association with acetaminophen-related communication enrichment and predicted matrix-remodelling RNA dynamics. By converting static ligand-receptor maps into velocity-constrained networks of signalling influence, CellVocal provides a general strategy for generating spatially resolved hypotheses about how intercellular communication contributes to predicted transcriptional changes.

papers.title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
papers.abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Detection of Maximal Exact Matches in Terabases of Genome Assemblies in Compressed Space and Sublinear Time
papers.abstract: Detection of long exact matches between a pair of genomes has historically been a fundamental operation in genomics. Similarly, detection of long exact matches between all pairs of haplotypes in a large panel of genotyping array data or whole-genome sequencing variant calls is a fundamental operation in population genetics. Thanks to various recent pangenome efforts, for the first time, large panels of high-quality genome assemblies are being constructed. Therefore, we propose the intersection of these two approaches: detection of long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in panels of hundreds to thousands of high-quality assemblies. Since these datasets would contain trillions of basepairs, practically detecting all exact matches requires algorithms operating in at most linear time and compressed space. Previous methods such as Mumemto achieve this, but running them on terabase-sized pangenomes still took very large space and long time. Here, we describe more efficient algorithms for outputting all long exact matches between all pairs of assemblies in compressed space and sublinear time given a compressed index of the panel. Given the construction of an O(r) space compressed index--a one-time cost that can be done in compressed space and close to linear time with previous work--we describe three algorithms taking O(r) words of memory: (1) computing all supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) in O(r) time, (2) computing all supermaximal exact matches and their occurrences in O(r + occ) time, and (3) computing all maximal exact matches (MEMs) in O(r + occ) time, where r is the number of runs in the Burrows-Wheeler transform of the panel of assemblies and occ is the number of occurrences or matches outputted. Our algorithms use 7.5 times less memory than state-of-the-art competitors on a dataset of human centromere assemblies from 625 haplotypes. They are also 20 times faster if index construction time is counted, and 2,500 times faster if index construction is excluded. Finally, we perform an analysis of all-vs-all MEMs in all well-assembled centromeres of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset that reveals multiple novel insights into structural variation in centromeres. For example, we find that the active -satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) array of Chromosome 2 is flanked by a ~200 kbp inversion on one side and a ~200-300 kbp pseudopalindromic sequence on the other. We also detect large segmental duplications in the centromere of every chromosome except Chromosome Y. These segmental duplications range in size from hundreds of kbp to multiple Mbp and occur both in and out of the active -satellite HOR arrays. Our computational results make pairwise MEM analyses possible in pangenomes, while our biological results show they are likely to be useful. Our algorithms are implemented as TeraMEM in the TeraTools suite available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.

papers.title: Pocket similarity guided selection of protein targets for systematic protein ligand dataset generation
papers.abstract: The scarcity of large, diverse, and unbiased protein ligand binding datasets limits the performance of machine learning approaches in drug discovery, particularly for understudied proteins. The Target 2035 initiative aims to address this gap by generating open-access binding data for more than 2,000 human proteins, a goal whose value depends on maximizing the diversity of the selected targets. Because proteins with different folds can share chemically analogous binding sites, we reasoned that pocket similarity, rather than sequence or fold similarity, is the appropriate criterion for selecting representative targets that maximize coverage of the human pocketome. Here, we use PocketVec, an alignment-free descriptor of binding sites, to map the human globular pocketome, identifying 51,535 predicted druggable pockets across 15,559 proteins. A two level hierarchical clustering, first within protein families and then across the whole proteome, grouped these pockets into 1,865 clusters of chemically similar binding sites. After discarding 533 clusters containing pockets with known ligands, we selected the 100 most populated of the remaining 1,332 ligand free clusters and chose two high quality representative pockets per cluster, ranked by their resemblance to known ligand-binding sites. Finally, we implemented two complementary prioritization strategies, one favoring structurally unexplored proteins and the other proteins amenable to experimental follow up, and selected 200 pockets from 100 different clusters from each strategy, with 89 clusters in common. Both selections cover over 10,000 pockets in ~5,600 proteins, approximately 36% of the human proteins with annotated druggable pockets, which represents a 2.8- to 4.4-fold increase in the number of covered pockets, domains, and proteins than random selection baselines. This pocket based framework offers a principled strategy to select diverse targets for Target 2035 and other large scale protein ligand data generation efforts in chemical biology.

papers.title: Basic-peptide depletion and precursor masking in bottom-up proteomics
papers.abstract: Biomarker proteomics studies report protein identities at the canonical precursor level, yet the underlying mass-spectrometry evidence consists of peptides whose physicochemical properties may diverge from the annotated protein. We reanalyzed peptide-level evidence from public datasets with a proteoform-aware pipeline that maps detected peptides to canonical sequences under a five-level confidence taxonomy, computes sequence-derived physicochemical features for precursors, peptides, and detected regions, and tests class-composition bias against digestion-matched backgrounds. Across ten public studies spanning five result-file formats and 70,020 peptide-evidence rows, detected peptides are depleted in the basic isoelectric-point class relative to their own proteins' theoretical tryptic peptides (fixed-effect odds ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.44-0.46; leave-one-study-out envelope 0.44-0.49). The depletion is absent among fully tryptic peptides (OR 1.06) and concentrates in missed-cleavage peptides (OR 0.62-0.57), is invariant to detected-abundance stratification, and retains its direction under three independent pI-calculator models. Case studies reveal both directions of precursor-centric masking. Two orthogonal validations ground the framework: a digestion-free synthetic-peptide analysis (basic-class odds ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.71-0.76 under standard DDA) and a paired top-down benchmark, in which detected regions recover top-down sequence space (90% of spans overlapped) but do not delimit proteoform boundaries (8% containment). Pipeline, data, and code are public.

papers.title: Assessing the Capacity of Genomic Language Models to Generate Informative Embeddings of Viral Genome Fragments
papers.abstract: Genomic language models (gLMs) trained on large volumes of nucleotide sequences are becoming an alternative to classical methods in metagenomic analysis, particularly for studying genomic "dark matter". In this work, we investigate the ability of four gLMs (DNABERT-2, DNABERT-S, ViraLM, and Evo2-7B) to generate taxonomically informative vector representations of short viral genome fragments. We constructed a balanced reference dataset of viruses based on the ICTV Virus Metadata Resource and compared the representations generated by gLMs with conventional k-mer profiles and MinHash sketches using clustering and neighborhood-based metrics (adjusted Rand index (ARI), precision@k, and CROSS precision@k). On the reference dataset, three of the four gLMs outperformed the 4-mer profile in terms of ARI and precision@5 under the same evaluation protocol. The best performance was generally achieved by intermediate model layers. Conventional k-mer profiles consistently outperformed MinHash sketches. We further evaluated the methods on two viral orders (egoviruses and mriyaviruses) absent from the reference dataset, with model layers and k-mer lengths selected exclusively on the reference dataset. DNABERT-S showed the most consistently strong performance across these two orders, ranking first on mriyaviruses and second on egoviruses, while k-mer profiles with Jensen-Shannon distance remained competitive. We also observed the consistency of representations between forward fragments and their reverse complements. Overall, the best-performing gLMs surpassed conventional baselines, although their advantage depended on the dataset and evaluation metric. The consistently strong performance of DNABERT-S suggests a potential benefit of contrastive fine-tuning and indicates that larger models are not necessarily more effective for generating taxonomically informative representations.

papers.title: SIFT: Syncmer-Informed Selection of Haplotypes for T2T Imputation
papers.abstract: Genome patching improves the completeness of fragmented assemblies by filling unresolved gaps with sequences from reference genomes. Pangenome panels provide diverse candidate haplotypes for this task, but identifying suitable references efficiently becomes increasingly challenging as these panels grow. We present SIFT, a compressed indexing method for selecting reference haplotypes for genome patching with ImpuT2T. SIFT combines closed-syncmer parsing, phrase-level indexing, and pseudo-maximal exact match (pseudo-MEM) queries. Closed syncmers provide a context-independent parsing rule with bounded distances between consecutive selected positions, enabling consistent parsing of reference and query sequences. We demonstrate that two closed syncmers determine the distance at which they can occur consecutively in any string, so that equal substrings of two parses represent identical sequences and no gap sequence need be stored. SIFT indexes the reference parse and its reverse using run-length compressed suffix arrays and adapts the Boyer-Moore-Li search procedure to identify pseudo-MEMs between the reference parse and query parse. It then aggregates matching evidence to identify candidate reference haplotypes for downstream patching. This framework connects compressed sequence indexing with haplotype selection and provides a basis for querying large reference panels at the phrase level. SIFT is publicly available under the GNU license at https://github.com/EddieFerro/SIFT.

papers.title: EMtrace: offline nanopore metagenomics on a laptop for rapid viral diagnostics, genome recovery and 16S profiling
papers.abstract: Nanopore sequencers produce reads within minutes, but metagenomic analysis remains challenging where internet access is limited, data are sensitive or computing resources are modest. EMtrace is an offline pipeline that runs on a laptop during sequencing: it classifies MinKNOW reads, estimates taxon abundance by expectation-maximization (EM) and assembles reference-based consensus genomes. We benchmarked it against five virome and four 16S rRNA tools on simulated, mock-community and clinical data. On field isolates and 16 SARS-CoV-2 clinical samples, EMtrace had the highest species-level F1 score (1.00 and 0.97) and one false-positive species, against 3-7 for the comparators. It recovered divergent viruses as completely as ViMOP, and low-titre field libraries more completely, at [≥]99.7% identity. In replayed runs, it identified the target virus in the first 4,000-read batch (5-13 min). With a shared 16S reference, EMtrace reported two to three times fewer false-positive species than Emu.

papers.title: HV-MultiScaleGNN: A Multi-Scale Graph Neural Network Framework for Host-Virus Protein-Protein Interactions Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of HV-PPIs is essential for understanding viral infection mechanisms and for developing antiviral therapeutic discovery. However, the experimental identification process is often time-consuming and expensive, while many computational approaches depend on incomplete protein sequences, structural and interaction information. Here, we present HV-MultiScaleGNN, a topology-driven multi-scale GNN framework for HV-PPIs prediction that operates exclusively on the topology of a heterogeneous interaction network. The framework formulates HV-PPIs prediction as a heterogeneous link prediction problem by integrating the human interactome with experimentally validated HV-PPIs. HV-MultiScaleGNN systematically investigates three complementary graph representation strategies, viz. Local view, Global view and an integrated Local+Global view. The Local view employs one-hop relation-aware graph attention to model fine-grained neighbourhood interactions. The Global view captures higher-order structural dependencies through propagation-based neighbourhood aggregation. The integrated representation combines both views to jointly encode local connectivity and global topological context within a unified embedding space, enabling relation-specific link prediction without relying on sequence- or structure-derived features. Experiments on large-scale HV-PPIs datasets evaluate all three strategies using discrimination, calibration, and ranking metrics. The Local view achieved the best discriminative performance (AUROC = 0.9444, AUPRC = 0.9422), whereas the Global view exhibited the lowest ECE (0.0379). The integrated Local+Global view provided consistently strong predictive performance (AUROC = 0.9378, AUPRC = 0.9356). Comparative evaluation against representative graph representation learning methods showed competitive predictive performance. Furthermore, interfacial interactions were identified using protein-protein docking and atomistic-level understanding was explored. Moreover, GO and KEGG enrichment provided additional functional insights into the selected host proteins. The proposed framework enables systematic evaluation of complementary graph representation strategies for heterogeneous biological link prediction and helps experimental researchers to delineate novel HV-PPIs.

papers.title: Reticulation-Aware Dissimilarities for Phylogenetic Networks
papers.abstract: Dissimilarity measures play a critical role in phylogenetics. They help quantify the accuracy of inferences when the ground truth is known, allow comparisons of inferences obtained using different methods, and provide a tool for summarizing sets of phylogenies. A wide array of dissimilarity measures has been introduced for phylogenetic trees over the past half-century, and they vary in their mathematical properties, empirical behavior, and computational complexity. When the evolutionary history involves reticulate processes, such as hybridization and horizontal gene transfer, it is represented by phylogenetic networks. Although the study of phylogenetic network dissimilarity is less established than its tree counterpart, the past two decades have seen an increasing number of measures developed for phylogenetic networks. However, while some have established mathematical properties---for example, metricity on certain classes of phylogenetic networks---none properly separates reticulation disagreement from tree-like disagreement. This is the rationale behind the introduction of the hybrid ancestry error (HAE) measure by Dai and Molloy. The HAE measure, however, is too simplistic to distinguish different reticulation scenarios. In this work, we propose a novel family of network dissimilarity measures that explicitly account for reticulation differences while being more informative than HAE. We prove that our measures are pseudometrics on rooted binary phylogenetic networks on a fixed taxon set, with two instantiations yielding metrics on binary level-1 networks. Empirically, the measures remain sensitive to reticulation errors as network size grows and respond to changes in hybrid identity and parental placement. Calibration experiments further characterize the measures' behavior under network edits of various magnitudes. Data Availability: The dissimilarities are implemented in the PhyNetPy library, available at https://github.com/NakhlehLab/PhyNetPy. All the data simulated for the study is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23933421. Funding: This work was supported in part by the NSF grants DMS/NIGMS-2153704 and DBI-2420499. Declaration of AI-assisted technologies: During the preparation of this work, the authors used OpenAI's Codex (GPT-6 Astra) and Anthropic's Claude (Fable 5) to assist with editing manuscript text, developing proofs and analysis code, and preparing figures. The authors reviewed and edited the resulting material, verified the analyses, and take full responsibility for the content of this article.

papers.title: Cross-state representation learning enables prospective discovery of dynamic protein allosteric sites
papers.abstract: Allosteric regulation offers multifunctional induction in therapeutic interventions, yet conformational plasticity hinders computational identification of allosteric sites. Machine learning models rely on static holo (ligand-bound) structures, generalizing poorly to apo or substrate-bound states where binding pockets are transient or cryptic. We present AsBench2, a cross-state site-recognition benchmark, and AllositeUltra, a deep learning framework integrating multimodal protein representations (combining structure-aware language models with physical dynamics) and residue-guided candidate supplementation, effectively decoupling site detection from static pocket geometry. AllositeUltra demonstrates superior generalization, achieving Top-3 site recovery rates of 65.2% and 70.6% on apo and substrate-bound structures, respectively, representing relative improvements of 36.4% and approximately 50% over the best-performing baselines. Prospective application to MAGI2 identifies a previously unrecognized interdomain allosteric pocket, validated at atomic resolution through small-molecule screening and X-ray crystallography. Proteome-wide application yields a high-confidence atlas of targetable allosteric sites, bridging the gap between structural representation learning and prospective AI-driven drug discovery.

papers.title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.

papers.title: DaliScope: Distilling Biological Insights from Deep Structural Alignments
papers.abstract: Structural similarity searches reveal protein relationships that sequence alignments miss, but treating DALI results as isolated match lists misses deeper connections. We present DaliScope, an interactive Python framework that treats complete DALI target sets as structured populations for systematic analysis of protein structural neighbourhoods. DaliScope combines structural community detection with sequence profiling, Pfam annotation, residue mapping, and 3D visualization, enabling target sets to be subdivided and examined at the residue level. We demonstrate two applications. In a multidomain protein with sparse domain annotation, structural analysis uncovered previously unannotated domains. A structurally anchored HxD...H signature occurred in 697 of 1,093 Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains and in 15 domains lacking Pfam annotation; relaxing the central residue constraint recovered 96% of Pfam-annotated CUPIN domains among the DALI targets. In a second application, a DALI search with transitive closure returned >12,000 hits. Applying an 80% coverage criterion to a conserved structural core reduced this set to 6,708 domain instances, resolved into 23 structural communities. (80% was chosen instead of the default 50% because the GOLD domain has a compact core with short loops.) Many communities were strongly enriched for individual Pfam families while providing structural context for 1,097 targets lacking Pfam assignments. Three-dimensional superimposition revealed structural continuity among related {beta}-sandwich architectures through progressive changes in sheet geometry and auxiliary elements. Together, these examples show how a single DALI query provides a structural anchor for organizing large neighbourhoods, extending interpretation beyond sequence-based annotations, and deriving structurally anchored sequence signatures from defined populations.

papers.title: Automated Continuous LLM-driven Biomedical Literature Mining for a Large-Scale Hepatotoxicity Knowledge Base
papers.abstract: Predicting whether a chemical disturbs liver and mitochondrial function matters for drug safety and environmental risk assessment, but the data available for training such models are small and mostly curated by hand. We describe an automated pipeline that uses a large language model (LLM) to collect hepatotoxicity findings from the biomedical literature. The pipeline runs a PubMed/PMC query, downloads the matching full texts or abstracts, asks the LLM to record each reported effect in a fixed schema (tested chemical, biomarker, direction of change, and related fields) with controlled vocabularies, and writes de-duplicated records to a database that is updated as new papers appear. The current snapshot holds 189,212 findings on 17,002 chemicals from 53,575 articles (1995-2026), covering 235 biomarkers reported for at least 20 chemicals. In a manual check of 217 findings from 35 articles, 208 findings (from 33 articles) were fully correct; the other 9, all from 2 articles, were incorrect. As a use case, we train structure-based QSAR models, both graph neural networks and classic baselines, for each biomarker; at this data scale the classic models remain competitive. The pipeline and the knowledge base will be made publicly available.

papers.title: ProClust provides reliable statistical significance of clusters for single-cell transcriptomic data
papers.abstract: Clustering of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is widely used to identify cell populations. However, overclustering can partition a single cell population into multiple clusters, potentially leading to spurious identification of cell subpopulations. Assessing the statistical significance of clusters is therefore needed to support their biological interpretation. We propose ProClust, a statistical test for clustering significance in scRNA-seq data. ProClust defines a single cluster as a log-concave distribution and adopts a projection-based approach to quantify clustering uncertainty through p-values. These projections can also provide interpretable visual evidence for individual clusterings. ProClust merges clusters when there is insufficient evidence to reject the single-cluster null hypothesis, refining an initial overclustering without prespecifying the final number of clusters. Across parametric and PBMC-based semi-synthetic simulations, ProClust avoided false subdivisions under single-population null settings while consistently recovering the underlying population structure across different numbers of true populations. In real scRNA-seq datasets from the Human Lung Cell Atlas, Tabula Muris, and Hydra, ProClust produced clustering solutions that showed overall agreement with reference annotations while retaining supported substructure and merging groups with insufficient evidence for separation. Together, these results demonstrate that ProClust provides a statistically principled and interpretable framework for refining an initial overclustering and distinguishing supported cellular heterogeneity. The ProClust R package is available at https://github.com/Anonym027/ProClust.

papers.title: Batch, Prefetch, Skip, Orient, Squeeze: Faster, Smaller k-mer dictionaries via the Spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform
papers.abstract: Looking up k-mers in an index is a core operation in genomics, underlying read mapping, metagenomic classification, and many other tasks. Queries are often streaming: the k-mers come from a longer sequence such as a sequencing read, and consecutive k-mers overlap. The fastest index for such queries is currently the hashing-based SSHash; indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) are competitive in space but slower. We show how to make SBWT indexes both faster and smaller. First, we process queries in small batches and prefetch the memory each will need next, hiding the latency of the dependent random accesses that dominate a lookup; together with a new rank structure that reads one cache line per query, this makes k-mer lookups about seven times faster than unbatched SBWT search. Second, we extend batching to streaming search and show that one failed lookup can rule out many k-mers of a read at once, which removes the need for the longest common suffix array. Third, we build an SBWT that stores only one orientation of each k-mer, thereby halving its size, with a modified search that exploits how rarely the orientation changes along a read. Finally, we adapt a compact subset rank structure to batched search. On the collections of the SSHash benchmark, and on two collections up to 15 times larger, our fastest index answers streaming queries for 31-mers faster than SSHash on every read set, by up to 4.9 times, using 12 bits per canonical k-mer against SSHash's 7.4-11.1. We also show that a 6.1-bit index is still faster than SSHash on most read sets, and that our smallest index needs about 4 bits per canonical k-mer. Unlike that of SSHash, the space of our indexes barely varies across collections. Our code is available at https://github.com/anadis504/sbwt-squeeze-rs.

papers.title: OmniT2I: a unified table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference with incomplete multimodal cancer data
papers.abstract: Molecular profiles and histopathology provide complementary information about cancer prognosis, but these data are often incomplete for individual patients. Here we present OmniT2I, a table-to-image framework for survival prediction and cross-modal inference from incomplete multimodal cancer data. Each molecular profile was converted into a three-channel image representation with correlation-based feature placement. OmniT2I combines available molecular and histopathology embeddings through availability-aware fusion and predicts missing modalities from those observed. Across 10,373 patients with 32 cancer types, the C-index was 0.631 within cancer types and 0.783 with all cancers pooled (0.660 and 0.787 in 5,605 patients with all five modalities). A single model handled all 31 modality combinations and, compared with nine survival methods trained separately for each, achieved higher C-indices in 240 of 279 pooled and 226 of 279 within-cancer comparisons. Adding predictions of withheld modalities to observed inputs improved pooled C-indices in all 180 pairings of observed and withheld modality sets and within-cancer C-indices in 164. Adding measured histopathology to RNA produced the largest within-cancer C-index gain among the four additional modalities evaluated, whereas adding copy number variation reduced it. In seven external cohorts, frozen RNA-only C-indices differed from test performance in the corresponding cancer type in TCGA by a median of -0.003 (range, -0.092 to +0.079). OmniT2I enables prognostic modeling with incomplete multimodal data.

papers.title: Integrating evolutionary and protein language model representations for thermodynamically consistent stability prediction
papers.abstract: At fixed thermodynamic conditions, protein stability changes obey reversal antisymmetry and path independence, but learned predictors need not satisfy these properties. Explicit alignment-derived evolutionary information may also complement single-sequence protein language model representations, motivating their integration under clearly defined physical constraints. Here, we develop a training-free strategy that combines thermodynamic constraints with complementary sequence representations. We first introduce EvoPhi-DDG, a potential-based adaptation of the alignment-conditioned evolutionary predictor MSAesm_ddG. By antisymmetrizing its predictions and setting the hidden biases to zero, we express stability changes as differences of a learned, evolution-informed effective potential conditioned on the mutation site and alignment context. This guarantees exact reversal consistency and exact same-site transitivity under fixed alignment contexts while preserving predictive accuracy. We further extend the adapted predictor to multiple substitutions through a background-aware construction that preserves whole-variant antisymmetry. We then combine EvoPhi-DDG with the previously published JanusDDG using fixed, equal weight averaging to test predictive complementarity without additional training. The ensemble preserves exact antisymmetry and reduces multisite pathway-closure RMSE relative to JanusDDG across all evaluated path lengths. Furthermore, the ensemble outperforms both components on S669 and S96, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.59 and 0.55, respectively, compared with 0.55 and 0.52 for JanusDDG and 0.53 and 0.48 for EvoPhi-DDG. On the multiple-substitution benchmark PTmul-NR, the ensemble achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.66, improving on JanusDDG's 0.61 and matching the EvoPhi-DDG extension at the reported precision. Together, these findings distinguish two benefits: averaging complementary predictions improves accuracy, whereas the potential-based reformulation strengthens physical consistency. They support the integration of alignment-conditioned and single-sequence representations without additional training, while separating predictive improvements from mathematical guarantees.

papers.title: Parallel transcriptome profiling of soybean cyst nematodes (SCN) during a three-way interaction among SCN, soybean aphids, and soybean
papers.abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines (Ichinoe) (Rhabditida: Heteroderidae) is arguably the greatest yield-limiting factor for soybean (Glycine max [L.] Merr.) production in the United States. Previous research found that the impact of SCN infestation on yield is exacerbated during concurrent infestations with soybean aphids (SBA), Aphis glycines (Matsurmura) (Hemiptera: Aphididae). Although recent research has characterized the host root transcriptomic response during these infestations little is known about the corresponding in planta gene expression dynamics of either pest. This study examines the transcriptomic expression of SCN in soybean cultivars' roots under single or combined SBA infestations at two different time points: 5 and 30 days post-infestation (DPI). The SCN transcriptomics for SCN-susceptible (S) PI 518671 (Williams 82) cultivar reacted equivalently to both SCN and SCN + SBA treatments. However, transcriptomics in SCN-resistant (R) MN1806CN (H. glycines HG type 0/race 3 resistant) demonstrated an elevated significant expression pattern under the SCN + SBA combined treatment. During the early infestation period (i.e., sampled at 5 DPI), both S and R cultivars reacted similarly, irrespective of treatment conditions. The functional enrichment analysis of 1829 differentially expressed genes/transcripts showed that during the early co-infestation period (5 DPI), SCN genes were significant and mapped towards resistance breakage, whereas in the late stage (30 DPI), the gene flux oriented towards nematode dormancy. Together, these results suggest that SCN activity is amplified when combined with SBA, offering foundational data for molecular breeding to produce SCN resistant soybean cultivars.

papers.title: Membrane Geometry Reveals Strengths and Limitations of AlphaFold-Predicted Transmembrane Protein Complexes
papers.abstract: High-confidence protein complex predictions do not necessarily represent physically or biologically plausible assemblies. This limitation is particularly relevant for transmembrane (TM) proteins, whose interactions are constrained by the lipid bilayer. Here, we systematically evaluated membrane compatibility in the recently expanded AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, analysing 189,469 high-confidence AlphaFold-Multimer TM-TM complexes and additional TM-soluble assemblies. Most predictions exhibited plausible membrane geometry: among 125,657 evaluable complexes with TM proteins possessing more than two TM helices, 95.4% had joint hydrophobic thicknesses within the expected range of 15-35 angstroms. Nevertheless, some complexes displayed substantial inconsistencies in membrane positioning or protomer orientation despite favourable prediction confidence. Interactions between TM proteins, particularly those containing only one or two TM helices, were frequently dominated by extramembrane contacts. Among TM-soluble complexes, 77.4% showed no penetration of the soluble partner into the hydrophobic membrane core. We further investigated whether AlphaFold3 (AF3) could overcome limitations of AlphaFold-Multimer. Although AF3 recovered an experimentally supported SERCA-phospholamban interaction, it failed to reproduce the cholesterol-mediated norepinephrine transporter homodimer. A benchmark of 173 cholesterol-containing membrane protein targets further revealed limited accuracy in predicting cholesterol-binding poses, particularly for structures released after the AF3 training cutoff. Together, these findings demonstrate that membrane-specific geometric constraints provide a valuable complement to conventional confidence metrics and highlight the persistent challenges of predicting assemblies involving lipids.

papers.title: LingoCell interprets gene perturbations through natural language and tissue niches
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models are general tools for resolving cell identities and disease states, but struggle to interpret changes in expression magnitude in biological language, to transfer to sparse spatial measurements, and to explain cellular niches. We introduce LingoCell, a foundation model connecting single-cell and spatial transcriptomics. It aligns cell representations with language while keeping gene expression editable, supporting cell annotation, cross-batch integration, description generation, and disease-language readouts of single-gene and combinatorial in silico perturbations. Extended to tissues, it annotates cells without single-cell references, learns identity-conditioned niche embeddings, and performs spatial in silico perturbation by replacing and editing neighbor expression. In lung adenocarcinoma, LingoCell revealed synergistic disease responses to jointly weakening alveolar differentiation programs and strengthening malignant programs. In colorectal cancer, it revealed different programs conveyed by the same fibroblast state to T cells, macrophages, and tumor cells. LingoCell provides a unified framework for prioritizing target combinations and stromal intervention programs.

papers.title: spSheaf: sheaf-theoretic spatial domain inference from raw molecules without cell segmentation
papers.abstract: Spatial-transcriptomics pipelines usually require cell segmentation and discard 20-60% of transcripts. We introduce spSheaf, a segmentation-free spatial domain inference method built on cellular sheaf theory. Within a domain, neighbouring regions have compatible local expression structure; across a transition between programs they remain discordant after alignment of their local subspaces. spSheaf quantifies this alignment-adjusted disagreement and attenuates transitions during clustering. On the MERFISH hypothalamus benchmark it attains mean ARI 0.571 and NMI 0.655, ranks first of twelve on NMI, and leads SSAM, Points2Regions and FICTURE by 0.16 ARI on held-out slices. On three further annotated sections, every method tuned, it leads on one, ties on one and trails SSAM by 0.06 ARI. The sheaf weighting adds +0.102 ARI where domains are distinct programs and is neutral on laminar cortex. One domain above the annotated count, it divides the BST into the territories of two atlas neuronal populations on both adjacent sections.

papers.title: Uncovering Viral Signals Across Cell Populations in Colorectal Cancer
papers.abstract: Viral sequences have been detected in colorectal cancer, but their cellular and anatomical distribution remains poorly resolved. We aimed to establish a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon. We repurposed human-unmapped reads from single-cell RNA sequencing libraries generated in ten publicly available studies. We retained cell-barcode and unique molecular identifier information, removed duplicate molecules, and aligned reads to a curated human-associated viral reference using three aligners. Viral signals were analysed across cell types, tissue conditions, and colorectal segments. We used participant-grouped repeated cross-validation to evaluate tissue-condition classification and screened an independent paired colorectal cancer proteomics cohort for compatible peptide matches. The study included 547 libraries from 112 participants, including 49 with matched colorectal cancer and tumour-adjacent normal samples, and approximately 415,000 cells spanning ten major cell populations. Viral reference-associated RNA signals differed across epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular compartments, tissue conditions, and anatomical regions of the colon. Of 318 independent healthy-reference viral-load comparisons, seven involving six virus-cell-type groups remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction, including plasma-cell HHV-7 and HHV-6B and mast-cell HCV-2. Cell-type-resolved viral features distinguished colorectal cancer, tumour-adjacent normal tissue, and healthy colon in participant-grouped validation; random forest achieved a macro-AUC of 0.957 (SD 0.028), with HERV-K113 as the leading quantitative feature. An independent proteomic screen identified peptide matches compatible with 20 candidate viral groups. We established a cell-type-resolved map of viral reference-associated RNA signals across colorectal tissue conditions and anatomical regions. By identifying candidate viral signals in epithelial and immune compartments, this map provides a basis for investigating virus-host pathways involved in tumour biology, immune regulation, and antigen-presentation states, and could help prioritise future combination strategies pairing virus-directed or virus-mimetic approaches with standard treatment or immune checkpoint blockade.

papers.title: CPDD: Adapting an autoregressive DNA language model for bidirectional phage genome modeling
papers.abstract: Autoregressive DNA language models generate sequences ef[fi]ciently from left to right, but many genome-analysis and sequence-editing problems are naturally conditioned on both [fl]anks. We introduce CreatiPhage, a 144.5M-parameter autoregressive DNA language model for bacteriophages, and its diffusion extension, CreatiPhage Diffusion DNA-LM (CPDD). CPDD is a 147.5M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model initialized from the six-epoch CreatiPhage checkpoint. CPDD retains the pretrained Transformer, block attention residuals, and Engram conditional memory, while introducing non-causal attention, a MASK-aware base-5 Engram, centered depthwise convolution, and position-aligned nucleotide readout. Training combines masked and GIDD-style uniformly substituted bases with nucleotide- and amino-acid-level losses over a 10 kb, 32 kb, and whole-source context curriculum. On a screened panel of 522 phage CDSs, CPDD achieves higher random-mask restoration accuracy than a comparable diffusion model and performs well above codon-level references. In a mixed-corruption test, it restores 42.4% of visible incorrect bases. Frozen CPDD representations also support infA [fi]tness prediction and seven-class phage virion protein subtype classi[fi]cation. Controlled evaluations further characterize how restoration depends on visible context and identify opportunities to improve longer-range sequence recovery. Together, these results support scaffold-conditioned sequence modeling as a step towards modular design of phage genomes.

papers.title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units--cells, bins or multicellular spots--into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p-values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene-gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p-values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.

papers.title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
papers.abstract: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.
